screens.title: Control Structures and Loops
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we make control flow a reliable tool for your smart contracts. You will learn how conditional statements let a contract make decisions and how loops repeat work when appropriate. We focus on practical Solidity patterns: if, else if, else for branching; for and while for iteration; and the gas-aware choices you must make when loops touch storage. I’ll show concrete examples that compare a safe memory loop to a risky storage loop, and we’ll discuss common mistakes like infinite loops, off-by-one errors, and denial-of-service risks caused by unbounded iteration. You’ll also see safe alternatives such as pagination, the pull pattern, and using off-chain proof structures instead of on-chain iteration. By the end of this lesson you should be able to choose control structures that are correct and predictable, and design functions that avoid gas surprises. Think about a function that sums a few numbers versus one that tries to process thousands of stored entries — the right control structure changes how usable and secure your contract is. Ready to dive into conditional logic first and then iterate safely?

screens.title: Conditional Statements in Solidity
screens.narratorSegment: Conditional statements let your contract pick different paths based on boolean expressions. In Solidity, an if evaluates a condition and executes its block when true. An else if provides an additional check when the first condition is false. An else block catches all remaining cases. These constructs are essential for validating inputs, enforcing permissions, and controlling state transitions. For example, a function might check if a caller is an owner, then allow a privileged action; otherwise it returns a permission error. A concrete example from the chapter checks age and license status to decide eligibility. When you write conditionals, prefer clear, mutually exclusive conditions and cover edge cases explicitly. A common misconception is believing the order of conditions doesn't matter; it does when multiple conditions overlap. An else if chain short-circuits at the first true branch, so place more specific checks before broader ones. Also avoid complex expressions in a single if: split checks into named boolean variables when readability and auditing matter. Key takeaway: use if/else chains to make intent explicit, guard state changes robustly, and avoid leaving uncovered states that produce undefined behavior.

keyIdea.title: Conditional clarity
keyIdea.text: Write explicit, ordered conditions and short-circuit safely to prevent unexpected state transitions.

content.html:
Core Concept
Conditional Statements in Solidity
if, else if, else — precise branching for safe state changes
Definition template
Definition & rules
  • If executes when its boolean condition is true.
  • Else if runs if the prior if was false and this condition is true.
  • Else runs when no prior condition matched.
  • Order matters: place specific checks before general ones because chains short-circuit.
Common misconception
Assuming two overlapping conditions will both run. They won’t; only the first true branch executes.
Example
// Example of conditional statements
function checkEligibility(uint age, bool hasLicense) public pure returns (string memory) {
    if (age >= 18 && hasLicense) {
        return "Eligible to drive.";
    } else if (age >= 18 && !hasLicense) {
        return "Eligible by age, but needs a license.";
    } else {
        return "Not eligible to drive.";
    }
}
Guided checklist
  1. Define clear boolean variables when expressions are complex.
  2. Order checks from most specific to most general.
  3. Include an else branch for unexpected inputs when appropriate.
  4. Use require for hard validation in public entry points.
Key Takeaway

Make branch logic explicit and auditable. Short-circuiting is intentional — place specific checks first to avoid logic errors.

screens.title: If / Else Examples and Auditing Tips
screens.narratorSegment: When auditing conditionals, the goal is to make intent and failure modes visible. Use require to enforce preconditions at public function entries. For internal decision logic, prefer short boolean names like isOwner or hasCapacity to make branches self-documenting. A concrete pattern is checking that an address is non-zero, that a user isn’t already registered, and that capacity limits are respected before modifying storage. The chapter provides an addParticipant example that uses require for validation, demonstrating industry practice: fail early and clearly. A common misconception is that moving checks into nested conditionals is equivalent to upfront require checks. It is not: upfront requires stop execution and gas is reverted with a clear message, which simplifies reasoning and auditing. During reviews look for missing else branches, ambiguous boolean expressions, and logic that depends on mutable state without proper guards. As a final thought, always consider invariants — conditions that should always hold — and encode them with explicit checks so your contract fails fast and predictably when those invariants are violated. If / Else Examples and Auditing Tips means fail early with require, name booleans clearly, and encode invariants to make conditionals auditable and predictable.. In practical terms, readable checks, require statements, and guarding state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Definition
If / Else examples and auditing tips
Prefer require for upfront validation and clear failure messages
Example: addParticipant validation
// Validation pattern used in examples
function addParticipant(address _newParticipant) public {
    require(_newParticipant != address(0), "Invalid address.");
    require(!isParticipant[_newParticipant], "Already a participant.");
    require(participants.length < MAX_PARTICIPANTS, "Participant limit reached.");

    participants.push(_newParticipant);
    isParticipant[_newParticipant] = true;
}
This pattern fails early and makes the caller aware why the transaction reverted.
Audit checklist
  • Are all public entry points validated with require where necessary?
  • Do boolean expressions use clear variable names?
  • Are edge cases and else branches covered?
  • Do messages explain the failure reason to callers?
Pro tip

Use small, pure helper functions to evaluate complex conditions so they can be unit tested independently.

screens.title: For Loops and a Safe Memory Example
screens.narratorSegment: A for loop has three parts: an initialization, a condition, and an increment. Use for loops when you know or can determine the number of iterations ahead of time. In Solidity, iterating over memory or calldata arrays is commonly acceptable for small sizes because they are cheaper than reading from storage repeatedly. The chapter’s sumArray example iterates a memory array and returns the summed total. That is an appropriate use: the caller provides the array and the gas cost is proportional to its size, but the array is not stored on-chain. A frequent misconception is that for loops are always safe. They are not when iterating storage arrays that can grow without bound. Another important point is off-by-one errors: use i < length rather than i <= length unless you explicitly need the last index, otherwise you risk out-of-bounds access. In practice, prefer small, fixed-size loops or validate a maximum input size before looping. This keeps gas predictable and avoids transactions that might run out of gas mid-execution. For Loops and a Safe Memory Example means use for loops for bounded iteration and prefer memory/calldata arrays or fixed-size loops to keep gas predictable.. In practical terms, when to use for loops and why memory arrays are cheaper. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow
For loops and a safe memory example
Initialization; condition; increment — predictable when bounded
Structure
  1. Initialize a loop counter (e.g., uint i = 0).
  2. Provide a terminating condition (e.g., i < length).
  3. Increment or decrement the counter each iteration.
Common mistake
Using <= where < is required, causing out-of-bounds access or unexpected extra iteration.
Example: sumArray (memory)
// Example of a for loop (use with caution for dynamic arrays in storage)
function sumArray(uint[] memory _arr) public pure returns (uint total) {
    for (uint i = 0; i < _arr.length; i++) {
        total += _arr[i];
    }
    return total;
}
This function is safe for small memory arrays because the caller controls the array size and the loop is bounded.
Key Takeaway

Prefer bounded memory loops. Validate maximum sizes when loops depend on external input.

screens.title: While Loops and Their Risks
screens.narratorSegment: A while loop repeats as long as a given condition remains true. It's useful when the number of iterations depends on a dynamic condition rather than a known count. In Solidity, however, while loops are less common because they can be harder to reason about and more likely to produce infinite loops if the loop condition doesn't reliably become false. The chapter’s countdown example decrements a local variable until zero and is safe in that controlled context. The primary risk is unbounded or user-controlled conditions that keep the loop running, which will consume gas until the transaction reverts. A misconception is believing that a while loop is inherently cheaper than a for loop; cost depends on the number of iterations and the operations inside each iteration. To use while loops safely, ensure the loop has a clear termination condition, limit maximum iterations with a separate guard, or avoid them in public functions that could be manipulated by malicious input. Always reason about worst-case iteration counts and consider alternative designs that split work into multiple calls or use off-chain helpers. While Loops and Their Risks means while loops must have reliable termination and guarded maximum iterations; otherwise they risk gas exhaustion and reversion.. In practical terms, when a while loop makes sense and how to avoid infinite loops. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition
While loops and their risks
Dynamic-condition repetition — verify termination
Example: countdown
// Example of a while loop (use with care)
function countdown(uint start) public pure returns (uint) {
    uint current = start;
    while (current > 0) {
        // In a real contract, this would perform some action
        current--;
    }
    return current; // will be 0
}
This is safe because the loop body reduces current and termination is guaranteed by the input magnitude.
Safety checklist
  • Prove the loop condition becomes false in all cases.
  • Add an explicit iteration cap if the condition can depend on external input.
  • Avoid while loops in functions that process untrusted user data without bounds.
Common mistake

Assuming termination without proving it. An infinite while loop will exhaust gas and revert the transaction.

screens.title: Storage vs Memory Iteration: Gas Implications
screens.narratorSegment: The crucial gas distinction is whether a loop reads from storage or from memory/calldata. Storage reads and writes are expensive on the EVM, so iterating a dynamic storage array inside a transaction grows gas linearly with the number of elements and can easily hit the block gas limit. The chapter gives the concrete case of summing a public storage array of user balances — this is risky when the array can grow large. Compare that to summing a memory array provided by the caller: memory accesses are cheaper and the caller controls the size, making costs more predictable. Common failure modes include transaction reversion when gas runs out, and denial of service if a malicious actor forces large iteration counts. Practical mitigations include pagination, pull mechanisms, processing in small chunks across multiple calls, and off-chain processing that submits compact proofs. A common misconception is thinking gas cost is a minor operational detail — in smart contracts it can change whether a function is usable at all. Always estimate worst-case gas and avoid public functions whose costs depend on untrusted inputs.

content.html:
Comparison
Storage vs Memory Iteration
Cost grows fast when loops read/write storage
Memory / Calldata loops
  • Caller supplies data; contract iterates a memory array.
  • Gas cost proportional to provided size; predictable if you limit input size.
  • Good for small aggregation tasks like summing a short array.
Storage loops
  • Iterating dynamic storage arrays reads expensive slots each iteration.
  • Risk: hit block gas limit and revert the transaction.
  • DoS risk: untrusted input can force long iterations.
Mitigation patterns
Pagination: split processing into pages
Pull pattern: users claim their share
Off-chain processing + proofs

screens.title: Safer Patterns: Pagination and Pull
screens.narratorSegment: When you must handle many items, split the work into smaller, predictable operations. Pagination means processing a slice of items per call — for example, process 50 participants at a time — so each transaction stays within gas limits. The pull pattern transfers responsibility to individual users: instead of the contract looping to pay everyone, each user calls claimReward and pays gas for their own claim. This spreads gas across participants and avoids single-call failures. The chapter suggests external iteration and relayers as another option: off-chain actors iterate large lists and submit compact results on-chain. A common misconception is that pushing responsibility to users is always less user-friendly. While it can add steps, it increases scalability and security by preventing malicious actors from forcing expensive on-chain work. When designing pagination or pull flows, include clear bounds, consistent indexing, and reentrancy protections where funds are transferred. These patterns trade developer complexity for predictable gas and robust on-chain availability. In practical terms, break work into small transactions and distribute gas responsibility. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Design trade-off
keyIdea.text: Split heavy processing into bounded calls or let users claim to avoid single-point gas failures and provide scalable access.

content.html:
Process Flow
Pagination and Pull Patterns
Design choices to manage gas for large data sets
Pagination
Process a limited number of items per transaction. Maintain a cursor or page index and let an external actor advance pages. This ensures each transaction stays under the gas limit and is retryable if partial work succeeds.
Example constraints
  • Define page size (e.g., 50 items)
  • Validate page index bounds
  • Emit progress events for off-chain monitoring
Pull pattern
Users claim values individually, paying gas themselves. The contract keeps balances and exposes claim functions. This scales naturally because cost is distributed across claimers.
Design notes
  • Store owed balances per user
  • Protect transfers with reentrancy guards
  • Prefer pull when the receiver is known and claimable

screens.title: Off-chain Iteration and Merkle Trees
screens.narratorSegment: For very large datasets, move heavy computation off-chain. External agents can iterate, compute results, and submit compact proofs or batched updates to the contract. Merkle trees are a canonical design for proving membership without iterating: the contract stores a Merkle root and users provide a proof of inclusion when claiming. This avoids on-chain loops entirely and keeps gas low. The chapter lists Merkle trees as an alternative to iterating whitelists. A common misconception is that proofs are always more complex than iteration; while they require initial setup and off-chain tooling, they make on-chain operations predictable and cheap. When using off-chain approaches, ensure the contract validates any submitted proof or batch atomically and that data integrity can be audited. If you track indices, update the moved element's index. If not, you may need to search for the index first, which is O(n).
getFirstNWhitelisted pattern
// Return first _n addresses (bounded)
function getFirstNWhitelisted(uint _n) public view returns (address[] memory) {
    require(_n > 0, "_n must be positive");
    uint count = _n < whitelistedAddressesArray.length ? _n : whitelistedAddressesArray.length;
    address[] memory slice = new address[](count);
    for (uint i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        slice[i] = whitelistedAddressesArray[i];
    }
    return slice;
}
Ensure _n is bounded and document maximum gas cost for callers. This pattern intentionally limits iteration to a safe size.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Defensive Checks
screens.narratorSegment: Developers commonly trip over a few recurring mistakes when working with control structures in smart contracts. Off-by-one errors in loop bounds can skip elements or access out-of-range indices; always prefer i < length and test boundary cases. Infinite loops arise when termination conditions are not guaranteed—never rely on mutable external state to reduce a loop counter unless you can prove termination. Unbounded iteration over storage is another frequent problem that leads to transaction reversion when gas runs out, and can be exploited for denial-of-service. Defensive checks you should add include maximum iteration caps, require guards on user-provided sizes, and clear error messages to help callers understand failures. For functions that transfer value, include reentrancy protections and update state before external calls. When designing public APIs, document worst-case gas scenarios and provide alternative flows for large workloads. A final practical tip: include unit tests that simulate large array sizes and boundary conditions so you catch gas and off-by-one issues before deployment. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we make control flow a reliable tool for your smart contracts. You will learn how conditional statements let a contract make decisions and how loops repeat work when appropriate. We focus on practical Solidity patterns: if, else if, else for branching; for and while for iteration; and the gas-aware choices you must make when loops touch storage. I’ll show concrete examples that compare a safe memory loop to a risky storage loop, and we’ll discuss common mistakes like infinite loops, off-by-one errors, and denial-of-service risks caused by unbounded iteration. You’ll also see safe alternatives such as pagination, the pull pattern, and using off-chain proof structures instead of on-chain iteration. By the end of this lesson you should be able to choose control structures that are correct and predictable, and design functions that avoid gas surprises. Think about a function that sums a few numbers versus one that tries to process thousands of stored entries — the right control structure changes how usable and secure your contract is. Ready to dive into conditional logic first and then iterate safely?

These objectives guide our practical work. First, you will implement conditional logic using if, else if, and else so your contracts can make clear decisions. You will see examples where conditions guard transfers or check deadlines, and you’ll learn how missing branches can produce unexpected behavior. Second, you will understand and apply for and while loops for iterative tasks, distinguishing when iteration is safe in memory or calldata versus when it touches storage and becomes expensive. Third, you will recognize the gas cost implications of loops, particularly for dynamic storage arrays. We’ll practice reasoning about block gas limits and how an unbounded loop can cause transaction reversion or denial of service. Fourth, you will identify and avoid common pitfalls—off-by-one errors, infinite loops, and iterating over large collections—and design functions that safely process data using pagination, pull patterns, or off-chain proofs. Each skill is paired with a small code example or design pattern you can try in your lab. By mastering these objectives you’ll write control flow that is correct, efficient, and predictable on-chain.

This second objectives slide maps what you will practice in the hands-on lab. You will implement a WhitelistManager that tracks addresses with a mapping and an array. You will practice safe adds and removes without iterating the full list in a single call. You will design remove operations using swap-and-pop to keep operations constant time. You will implement a getFirstNWhitelisted function to demonstrate safe, bounded iteration and to highlight why iterating over all entries is risky when a list grows. Each objective ties back to gas-awareness: limits, constant-time operations, and avoiding loops whose cost depends on untrusted input. The lab also reinforces the pull versus push design decision so you can reason about distributing rewards safely. By practicing these skills you’ll be ready to decide when a loop is acceptable and when a different architecture is required.

Conditional statements let your contract pick different paths based on boolean expressions. In Solidity, an if evaluates a condition and executes its block when true. An else if provides an additional check when the first condition is false. An else block catches all remaining cases. These constructs are essential for validating inputs, enforcing permissions, and controlling state transitions. For example, a function might check if a caller is an owner, then allow a privileged action; otherwise it returns a permission error. A concrete example from the chapter checks age and license status to decide eligibility. When you write conditionals, prefer clear, mutually exclusive conditions and cover edge cases explicitly. A common misconception is believing the order of conditions doesn't matter; it does when multiple conditions overlap. An else if chain short-circuits at the first true branch, so place more specific checks before broader ones. Also avoid complex expressions in a single if: split checks into named boolean variables when readability and auditing matter. Key takeaway: use if/else chains to make intent explicit, guard state changes robustly, and avoid leaving uncovered states that produce undefined behavior.

When auditing conditionals, the goal is to make intent and failure modes visible. Use require to enforce preconditions at public function entries. For internal decision logic, prefer short boolean names like isOwner or hasCapacity to make branches self-documenting. A concrete pattern is checking that an address is non-zero, that a user isn’t already registered, and that capacity limits are respected before modifying storage. The chapter provides an addParticipant example that uses require for validation, demonstrating industry practice: fail early and clearly. A common misconception is that moving checks into nested conditionals is equivalent to upfront require checks. It is not: upfront requires stop execution and gas is reverted with a clear message, which simplifies reasoning and auditing. During reviews look for missing else branches, ambiguous boolean expressions, and logic that depends on mutable state without proper guards. As a final thought, always consider invariants — conditions that should always hold — and encode them with explicit checks so your contract fails fast and predictably when those invariants are violated. If / Else Examples and Auditing Tips means fail early with require, name booleans clearly, and encode invariants to make conditionals auditable and predictable.. In practical terms, readable checks, require statements, and guarding state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A for loop has three parts: an initialization, a condition, and an increment. Use for loops when you know or can determine the number of iterations ahead of time. In Solidity, iterating over memory or calldata arrays is commonly acceptable for small sizes because they are cheaper than reading from storage repeatedly. The chapter’s sumArray example iterates a memory array and returns the summed total. That is an appropriate use: the caller provides the array and the gas cost is proportional to its size, but the array is not stored on-chain. A frequent misconception is that for loops are always safe. They are not when iterating storage arrays that can grow without bound. Another important point is off-by-one errors: use i < length rather than i <= length unless you explicitly need the last index, otherwise you risk out-of-bounds access. In practice, prefer small, fixed-size loops or validate a maximum input size before looping. This keeps gas predictable and avoids transactions that might run out of gas mid-execution. For Loops and a Safe Memory Example means use for loops for bounded iteration and prefer memory/calldata arrays or fixed-size loops to keep gas predictable.. In practical terms, when to use for loops and why memory arrays are cheaper. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A while loop repeats as long as a given condition remains true. It's useful when the number of iterations depends on a dynamic condition rather than a known count. In Solidity, however, while loops are less common because they can be harder to reason about and more likely to produce infinite loops if the loop condition doesn't reliably become false. The chapter’s countdown example decrements a local variable until zero and is safe in that controlled context. The primary risk is unbounded or user-controlled conditions that keep the loop running, which will consume gas until the transaction reverts. A misconception is believing that a while loop is inherently cheaper than a for loop; cost depends on the number of iterations and the operations inside each iteration. To use while loops safely, ensure the loop has a clear termination condition, limit maximum iterations with a separate guard, or avoid them in public functions that could be manipulated by malicious input. Always reason about worst-case iteration counts and consider alternative designs that split work into multiple calls or use off-chain helpers. While Loops and Their Risks means while loops must have reliable termination and guarded maximum iterations; otherwise they risk gas exhaustion and reversion.. In practical terms, when a while loop makes sense and how to avoid infinite loops. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The crucial gas distinction is whether a loop reads from storage or from memory/calldata. Storage reads and writes are expensive on the EVM, so iterating a dynamic storage array inside a transaction grows gas linearly with the number of elements and can easily hit the block gas limit. The chapter gives the concrete case of summing a public storage array of user balances — this is risky when the array can grow large. Compare that to summing a memory array provided by the caller: memory accesses are cheaper and the caller controls the size, making costs more predictable. Common failure modes include transaction reversion when gas runs out, and denial of service if a malicious actor forces large iteration counts. Practical mitigations include pagination, pull mechanisms, processing in small chunks across multiple calls, and off-chain processing that submits compact proofs. A common misconception is thinking gas cost is a minor operational detail — in smart contracts it can change whether a function is usable at all. Always estimate worst-case gas and avoid public functions whose costs depend on untrusted inputs.

When you must handle many items, split the work into smaller, predictable operations. Pagination means processing a slice of items per call — for example, process 50 participants at a time — so each transaction stays within gas limits. The pull pattern transfers responsibility to individual users: instead of the contract looping to pay everyone, each user calls claimReward and pays gas for their own claim. This spreads gas across participants and avoids single-call failures. The chapter suggests external iteration and relayers as another option: off-chain actors iterate large lists and submit compact results on-chain. A common misconception is that pushing responsibility to users is always less user-friendly. While it can add steps, it increases scalability and security by preventing malicious actors from forcing expensive on-chain work. When designing pagination or pull flows, include clear bounds, consistent indexing, and reentrancy protections where funds are transferred. These patterns trade developer complexity for predictable gas and robust on-chain availability. Safer Patterns: Pagination and Pull means split heavy processing into bounded calls or let users claim to avoid single-point gas failures and provide scalable access.. In practical terms, break work into small transactions and distribute gas responsibility. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

For very large datasets, move heavy computation off-chain. External agents can iterate, compute results, and submit compact proofs or batched updates to the contract. Merkle trees are a canonical design for proving membership without iterating: the contract stores a Merkle root and users provide a proof of inclusion when claiming. This avoids on-chain loops entirely and keeps gas low. The chapter lists Merkle trees as an alternative to iterating whitelists. A common misconception is that proofs are always more complex than iteration; while they require initial setup and off-chain tooling, they make on-chain operations predictable and cheap. When using off-chain approaches, ensure the contract validates any submitted proof or batch atomically and that data integrity can be audited. Developers commonly trip over a few recurring mistakes when working with control structures in smart contracts. Off-by-one errors in loop bounds can skip elements or access out-of-range indices; always prefer i < length and test boundary cases. Infinite loops arise when termination conditions are not guaranteed—never rely on mutable external state to reduce a loop counter unless you can prove termination. Unbounded iteration over storage is another frequent problem that leads to transaction reversion when gas runs out, and can be exploited for denial-of-service. Defensive checks you should add include maximum iteration caps, require guards on user-provided sizes, and clear error messages to help callers understand failures. For functions that transfer value, include reentrancy protections and update state before external calls. When designing public APIs, document worst-case gas scenarios and provide alternative flows for large workloads. Let's summarize the essentials. Conditional statements — if, else if, else — should be explicit, ordered from specific to general, and include guards for invalid inputs. For and while loops repeat work, but only use them when iteration counts are predictable or bounded; memory and calldata loops are cheaper than storage loops. Gas matters: iterating over large storage arrays can exceed block gas limits, cause reverts, and create denial-of-service vectors. Safer alternatives include pagination, the pull pattern, external off-chain processing, and Merkle proofs to verify membership without on-chain scanning. As a quick reference, keep three ideas in mind. First, conditionals must be explicit and ordered: place specific checks first and use require to fail fast with clear messages. Second, avoid unbounded storage loops: if you must iterate storage, do it in bounded slices or move processing off-chain. Third, prefer patterns that distribute gas cost: pull mechanisms and pagination scale better than a single transaction that tries to handle a large list. These three compact rules help you decide whether to write a loop, refactor to a pull model, or adopt off-chain proofs. When in doubt, ask: can a user or attacker enlarge the work the contract must do? If yes, redesign. That single question will keep your control structures safe and your contracts usable on-chain.
